judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard consideration-and-reliance preamble; no term in it carries competing meanings and nothing is enumerated against a catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its 'reliance upon the statements in the declarations' fits the Declarations Condition 12 but is qualified by the Wisconsin misrepresentation endorsements (c097/c117), a limitation rather than a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated list of payments with fixed caps ($250 per bail bond, $25 per day); each item is concrete, though 'all expenses incurred by the company' is open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item (c) (first aid expenses) is expressly cancelled for professional liability by the HPL First Aid Exclusion (c049) and by the Incidental Medical Malpractice coverage (c158), and c169 adds prejudgment interest, so the provision is only readable with those amendments.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A bare introductory line to the definitions; there is nothing to construe in it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states that definitions apply to endorsements, which is consistent with the many endorsements that redefine terms (e.g., c195 products hazard).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional definition with a clean carve-out for mobile equipment; the boundary is set by another defined term rather than left vague.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It dovetails with the mobile equipment definition (c012) and the loading/unloading definition (c168) without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Bodily injury ... which occurs during the policy period' is the classic trigger phrase whose application to progressive or latent injury is genuinely contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Broad Form endorsement (c158) amends this very definition to include Incidental Medical Malpractice Injury, and the HPL part covers 'injury' caused by a medical incident rather than bodily injury, leaving the two coverage parts using different injury concepts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The closing reference to 'an incident contract' is a mechanical slip for the defined 'incidental contract,' though the intended sense is recoverable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates with the explosion and underground hazard definitions (c009, c019) and CGL exclusion (q) (c130) without inconsistency; the hazard is remote from a hospital risk.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Arising out of operations of reliance upon a representation' is a garbled conjunction, and 'operations ... otherwise complete shall be deemed completed' leaves a fuzzy edge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It meshes with exclusion (q), the limits provisions and the products hazard definition; the redefinition endorsement (c195) touches products hazard, not this one.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A detailed definition with concrete exclusions and a measurable four-foot criterion; little room for competing readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supports CGL exclusion (l) (c125) and the Broad Form property damage carve-outs (c156) consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Structured inclusion/exclusion drafting; the only oddity is OCR corruption of 'independent contractors' rather than a substantive ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels the collapse and underground hazard definitions and is invoked only by exclusion (q) (c130), with no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A closed list of five written agreements invites an expressio unius fight about anything not listed, and the enumeration is the whole reach of the term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Broad Form endorsement expressly extends 'incidental contract' to any oral or written contract relating to the named insured's business, so the definition read literally contradicts the endorsement's extension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The severability sentence ('applies separately to each insured ... except with respect to the limits') is short and much-litigated in insurance practice.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It must be read with the multiple Persons Insured provisions (c043, c062, c131, c183) and with the aggregate limits (c044, c132), which it expressly does not multiply.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long but concretely itemised definition tied to registration and use tests; boundaries are objectively applied.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It functions as the complement of the automobile definition (c004) and is used in the CGL exclusions without inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line pointer to Item 1 of the declarations; nothing internally ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c092) and Endorsement 13 (c211) make a dozen entities 'named insureds' although they are not in Item 1, so the defined term and those endorsements pull apart.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The trailing 'other than such container, rented to or located for use of others but not sold' is a syntactically awkward exclusion whose reach is uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits alongside the products hazard definition, which is separately redefined by Form 009-136 (c195), but the products definition itself is untouched.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Neither expected nor intended from the standpoint of the insured' is one of the most litigated phrases in liability insurance and can be read subjectively or objectively.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Extended Bodily Injury endorsement (c162) expands 'occurrence' to include some intentional acts, and the limits endorsement (c167) supplies a separate aggregation rule, so three provisions govern the same word.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A structured three-branch geographic definition; each branch is concrete despite OCR damage.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Limited Worldwide Liability (c160) amends it, the HPL part states its own territory (c045), and Forms 009-118 (c172, c205) amend the HPL territory again, so several territory provisions coexist.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard products hazard wording with two cumulative conditions; the terms are technical but settled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Form 009-136 (c195) redefines 'products hazard' by dropping the 'away from premises' requirement for described premises/operations, leaving two definitions of the same term in the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The two-branch definition tying loss of use to an occurrence during the policy period is conventional, though 'tangible property' can be argued at the margin.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the property damage exclusions and the limits provisions; the nuclear endorsement (c201) expands it only for radioactive contamination.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An itemised hazard definition with a specific list of subterranean property and named operations; little interpretive slack.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is invoked only by exclusion (q)(3) (c130) and harmonises with the collapse and explosion hazards.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Machinery for computing premium by reference to the company's own rules is one-sided but administratively definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It refers to an 'audit period designated in the declarations' when the declarations designate none, and the Pay Plan endorsement (c113) substitutes an installment schedule for the deposit/earned premium mechanism.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear disclaimer of any inspection undertaking coupled with an audit right; both halves are definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It stands independently of the other conditions and is not amended by any Wisconsin endorsement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Conditional on certification under a motor vehicle financial responsibility law; the trigger and the reimbursement duty are both specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Amendment of Limits endorsement (c165) contains the matching proviso about separate limits under such laws, so the two are consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'As soon as practicable' and 'particulars sufficient to identify' are elastic standards that notice disputes routinely turn on.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This subsection is superseded twice — by the HPL Amended Condition 4 (c048) and again by the Wisconsin endorsement (c095, 'as soon as reasonably possible') — so which notice duty applies is genuinely uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete duty to forward demands 'immediately'; the obligation is plain even if timing is fact-bound.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is restated in the HPL Amended Condition 4 (c048), which replaces Condition 4 for professional liability, so the original survives only for other coverages.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cooperation duty and voluntary-payment bar are standard and specific, with a first-aid carve-out.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The HPL part replaces this condition wholesale (c048) and the First Aid Exclusion (c049) removes the first-aid carve-out for professional liability, so the two versions differ.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No action shall lie ... nor until the amount of the insured's obligation ... finally determined' is a definite condition precedent, though 'full compliance with all of the terms' is severe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Wisconsin Amendatory endorsement (c114) deletes this condition in its entirety and replaces it, while the Wisconsin Professional Liability endorsement (c098) says the condition 'does not apply' at all — three inconsistent instructions about the same condition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Primary insurance, except when stated to apply in excess' is definite on its face; the contribution machinery follows in (a) and (b).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Several endorsements make particular coverages excess and say the Other Insurance condition is 'amended accordingly' (c155, c157, c159, c186), so the primary/excess character varies coverage by coverage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An arithmetical sharing formula; mechanical rather than interpretive.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It operates only when the lead-in of Condition 6 (c027) applies, and the excess endorsements displace it for particular coverages.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A proportional limits formula stated as a ratio; definite in application.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Same relationship as (a): subordinate to Condition 6 and displaced where an endorsement makes a coverage excess.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional subrogation clause with a cooperation and no-prejudice duty; nothing ambiguous is named.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Wisconsin Amendatory endorsement (c115) adds a made-whole proviso that materially qualifies this clause, so the two must be read together.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain no-waiver/endorsement-only-change clause; the operative words are definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Both Wisconsin endorsements (c096 and c116) reverse its first sentence by imputing an agent's knowledge to the company, a direct contradiction of 'notice to any agent ... shall not effect a waiver.'

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is definite but drafted for a natural person ('shall die,' 'his duties'), which does not fit the corporate named insured.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The named insured is a corporation and the Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c092) lists entities, so the death-of-insured machinery has no application under this instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conditional rule for three-year policies, stated clearly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The declared policy period is one year (03/01/1996–03/01/1997), so this condition is inert surplusage rather than in conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The cancellation machinery is definite, with a stated thirty-day notice period.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Endorsement No. 4 (c069) requires sixty days' notice, the Cancellation–Wisconsin form (c107–c110) prescribes ten, forty and sixty day periods for different situations, and the Wisconsin Professional Liability endorsement (c099) restricts the grounds — four provisions govern the same subject with different numbers.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An integration and representation clause; the operative words are conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Both Wisconsin endorsements (c097 and c117) add a paragraph that sharply limits the effect of misrepresentation, altering the reliance premise of this condition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate attaching language; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches the endorsement's own stated effective date of 03/01/1996, so no tension arises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Unlicensed physicians,' 'rotate to,' and 'do not follow them with their respective coverages' are all undefined and their boundaries are genuinely uncertain, closed by the cryptic 'but not otherwise.'
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants employee-equivalent coverage to physicians while the Wisconsin Persons Insured provision (c056) excludes licensed physicians and the Medical Staff extension (c183) makes such coverage excess (c186), so the fit is awkward.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All sums ... because of injury ... caused by a medical incident which occurs during the policy period' packs the coverage trigger into one phrase that depends on the contested 'medical incident.'
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with the medical incident definition (c046), the per-incident limits (c044) and Additional Condition B (c050), and the increased-limits endorsement (c173) changes the money it promises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional employee-injury exclusion tied to course of employment; the terms are settled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The GL 00 32 endorsement (c170) deletes and replaces 'the exclusion relating to bodily injury to any employee of the insured' without saying which coverage part, and the Wisconsin Persons Insured provision (c056) carves back injury from professional services rendered to employees.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard workers' compensation exclusion; 'or under similar law' is a modest catch-all after named statutes.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels the CGL workers' compensation exclusion and the medical payments exclusion (c146(4)) with no inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Liability of an insured, if an individual, for such insured's personal acts or omissions involving a medical incident' is dense and its scope against individual insureds is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Two endorsements disapply it — the Wisconsin Persons Insured endorsement (c060) and the Medical Staff extension (c184) — leaving its residual field uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard auto/watercraft/aircraft exclusion listing the ownership-and-use verbs; definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Form 009-050 (c188) rewrites it to except professional health care services and deem patient loading a health care service, and Endorsement No. 5 (c071) amends that amendment again for air ambulances.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short three-part list of insureds with clear qualifiers.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Wisconsin Persons Insured endorsement (c051/c052) states that the persons insured provisions are 'changed to read as follows,' so this list is superseded while still printed in the coverage part.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The limit turns entirely on 'all injury arising out of any one medical incident,' which is precisely the aggregation question parties fight over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The declarations state $400,000 each incident with a $4,000,000 aggregate while the coverage part schedule states a $1,000,000 aggregate, and Form 009-123 (c173) raises limits to $1,000,000/$3,000,000 for insureds outside the Wisconsin Fund while c187 forbids increasing declared limits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is broken mid-sentence ('anywhere in the ___') and its proviso about where original suit must be brought is left dangling.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Two successive Form 009-118 endorsements (c172, c205) purport to amend this same territory provision by reciting a Wisconsin statute, and the first of them is later deleted (c203), so the operative territory text is uncertain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The closing sentence — 'any such act or omission together with all related acts or omissions ... to any one person shall be considered one medical incident' — makes everything turn on the undefined word 'related,' and 'professional health care services' is itself contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It drives the per-incident limit (c044) and the exclusivity clause (c050), and it must be reconciled with the separate 'occurrence' definition (c015) and the CGL aggregation rule (c167), which count losses on a different basis.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An inclusive definition tying 'suit' to arbitration in two defined situations; narrow and clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably with the defence obligation in c038 and with the Broad Form arbitration condition (c137).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any specific circumstances involving a particular person likely to result in a claim' is a notably vague reporting trigger, and 'as soon as practicable' compounds it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Wisconsin Professional Liability endorsement (c095) replaces the same Condition 4(a) with a different formula ('as soon as reasonably possible'), so two amended versions of the notice duty coexist for the same coverage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence exclusion of first-aid expense that expressly says the Supplementary Payments provision is amended accordingly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cancels item (c) of Supplementary Payments (c002) for this coverage part while the Incidental Medical Malpractice coverage (c158) does the same for the CGL side, which is coordinated rather than contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Except as stated in this Part, this policy does not apply to injury caused by any medical incident' is a sweeping one-sentence carve-out whose reach over the rest of the policy is genuinely arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It appears to negate the Broad Form Incidental Medical Malpractice Liability Coverage (c158), the Charitable Health Care Services extensions (c090/c196) and the Medical Staff extension (c183), all of which extend policy coverage to acts that are medical incidents.
